concepts.def: The smallest unit of life; carries out the functions needed to live.
A cell with a nucleus enclosed in a membrane; e.g. animal, plant, fungus cells.
A smaller cell with no nucleus; DNA is a loop in the cytoplasm; e.g. bacteria.
Parts inside a cell with specific jobs: nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, chloroplasts.
Cells adapted for a specific role, e.g. red blood cell, sperm, root hair.
Undifferentiated cell that can divide to form many cell types.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Organisation of the Organism — a core area of GCSE Biology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Organisation of the Organism brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Organisation of the Organism.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a prokaryote?
options: Human skin cell
Yeast
Bacterium
Onion cell
protein synthesis
photosynthesis
aerobic respiration
cell division

mcqs.q: What actually changes during natural selection in a population?
options: The frequencies of alleles in the population's gene pool change across generations.
Individual organisms change their own genes to adapt.
Enzymes choose their substrate based on which one is most common in the cell.
The entire DNA sequence of every individual changes simultaneously.

mcqs.q: Why are enzymes specific to certain substrates?
options: The entire DNA sequence of every individual changes simultaneously.
Only substrates with complementary shape and chemistry to the active site can bind effectively.
Each enzyme can react with any substrate, but works fastest with one type.
Enzymes choose their substrate based on which one is most common in the cell.

mcqs.q: Why is negative feedback the default mechanism in homeostasis?
options: Negative feedback amplifies changes to make them more noticeable.
The entire DNA sequence of every individual changes simultaneously.
Negative feedback only operates when something goes wrong in the body.
It opposes deviations from a set point, returning the variable toward its normal value — keeping internal conditions stable.
